question.text: The initial period of negative returns in the J Curve is primarily caused by:

answer.text: Management fees, organizational expenses, and unrealized investments being valued at cost while fees erode value

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook attributes the early negative J Curve phase to capital drawdowns, investments still being made, fees and expenses affecting returns, insignificant early distributions, and initial investments being carried at cost and revised later. NAV is pressured early because fees/expenses are incurred before realisations occur. The Trap: Option B aligns with the source-listed drivers. Market crashes, capital withdrawals, and policy changes are not the structural J Curve cause. Note: Earlier wording told distributors to position years 1-3 as the negative window and to reassure investors that the negative phase is "not a sign of poor management." Those are broader than the workbook unless tied to its illustrative J Curve figures and have been removed; the explanation now stays with source-backed fees/expenses/investment-period/NAV language.
